name: Jamal Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy hardware and fasteners for a building-supply distributor, screws, brackets, hinges, a few thousand lines in all. I'm in at seven, call two suppliers before the warehouse opens, then go through the weekly stock sheet with a pencil, because I trust my eyes more than the screen. At ten, my team of four and I argue about what to order for the spring rush. I've done this thirty-odd years and I'm good at it. What wears me out is the pressure to hit a margin number set by people who have never carried a box of bolts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, told you so. Plenty of hype and a few small savings, like auto-filling a purchase order. Down the pub I'd say the same, and I'd add that every year some consultant tells us the revolution has arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I still don't relax. Our margin target goes up every year no matter what, and I'm 58 with about four months in the bank. A quiet year is fine, but one bad restructure by the owners and I'm out whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now and push my retirement date to be sure of the pension. I'd keep the pencil stock sheet, keep the supplier calls, and put an extra 300 a month away. I might ask the union rep about our redundancy terms, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it feels fine, a bit flat. I like my work and I like being left alone to do it. Yet there's a low hum of worry that doesn't come from AI at all, it comes from the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your team. Who on that team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya is the youngest on my team, she's 26 and very good with the stock system. If the owners wanted to trim, she'd be the cheap one to keep and I'd be the expensive one to lose. That sits badly with me, because I trained her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep your routine. Is there anything in your week that you can already see a machine taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reorder emails, honestly. The software already drafts them and I tick yes. I'd be happy to hand that over, as long as nobody then says my time is worth less. A routine job done by software isn't my judgement.

say: I'd tell colleagues this is **hype** and the routine saving is small.
I'd say the real threat is **owners' margin targets**, not clever software.
think: I'm still worried: my **savings are thin** and one restructure could end my job anyway.
I fear the young colleague I trained would be **kept over me** because I cost more.
do: Keep **buying by phone** and pencil, exactly as now.
Put an extra **300 a month** towards my pension gap.
Ask the union rep about our **redundancy terms**.
feel: Mostly **flat and fine**, with a low hum of money worry.
S0.quote: I'm 58 with about four months in the bank. A quiet year is fine, but one bad restructure by the owners and I'm out whatever AI does.
fieldNote: He is calm about AI but **carries real money worry**, which colours everything he says.
Blames **owners' margin targets**, not technology, and names the younger colleague he trained as a worry.

steps.text: Keep buying hardware by phone and pencil sheet as usual
Put an extra 300 a month into the pension pot
Ask the union rep to confirm our redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the tail wagging the dog. The software will order the easy lines, and the company will say it's freed us for higher work, but the higher work is cheaper people babysitting the machine. I'd say that loudly in a meeting and quietly to my wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is mostly that thinking work, so I'm in the firing line. Not tomorrow, but the next time someone retires, they won't be replaced. I'd be one of the last who knows why we stock a certain brand of hinge, and I'm not sure that knowledge is wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay out of the tools as long as I decently can and focus on what the machine can't do: supplier relationships, the favours, knowing which rep lies. I'd also push the union to demand an agreement on what's automated and what happens to the people. And I'd start saving harder, maybe 500 a month, and look at leaving at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, I still feel I have some say, but my stomach tightens when I picture the Monday meeting where they announce a new system. I've seen it before with the old inventory software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called buying one of the tasks the card names. What exactly would go first in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reordering from the usual suppliers and chasing late deliveries. A machine can do that overnight. The price talks with a supplier who's behind on payment, no, I don't think it can do those, because it depends on who trusts whom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the tools. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'd get a proper pay deal and a no-compulsory-redundancy promise, I'd look at it. I'm not against learning, I'm against being used. Show me the machine is a help to my work, not a replacement dressed up, and a guarantee in writing, then I'll sit down with it.

say: I'd say software will take the **easy ordering** and the company will call it progress.
I'd demand the union get a **written agreement** on what's automated.
think: My job is mostly **thinking work**, so I'm exposed once colleagues retire unreplaced.
I doubt the machine can handle **supplier trust** and favours, but management may not care.
do: Stay off the tools and lean on my **supplier relationships**.
Push the union for a **no compulsory redundancy** deal.
Save **500 a month** and plan to leave at 60.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight stomach, but still feeling some control.
S1.quote: I'm not against learning, I'm against being used.
fieldNote: His resistance is **conditional, not stubborn**: it depends on written guarantees.
He sees his **supplier-trust knowledge** as his protection and wonders whether management values it.

steps.text: Lean on supplier relationships the software can't copy
Push the union for a written no-forced-redundancy deal
Save 500 a month and plan to leave at 60

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a catastrophe for ordinary people, and that governments and companies have had years of warning and done nothing. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it online, which I never do. This isn't hype, it's a few people deciding for everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished in this job by 2028. Everything I do is thinking work, and AI would do all of it better and cheaper. The robots arrive three years later and that hits the warehouse lads I've worked with for decades. Nobody I know has a plan, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go through every expense and cut it, the holiday, the car swap. I'd ask for a meeting about early retirement and severance while the company still needs me. I'd push the union hard for an agreement. And I'd tell my kids to stop counting on any help from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd lie awake doing sums on what four months' savings does against twelve years until the full pension. My wife would tell me to breathe, and she'd be right, but it doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you do in the first week after hearing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a meeting with my team of four that same week and tell them plainly what I think. They deserve not to be surprised. Then I'd go to the owners and ask what they plan. I won't pretend, whatever the company line is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your pension. What would you need to hold on to, concretely, to get through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bridge, nothing more. Income from now to the day the pension starts, and the health cover that goes with it. If the state or the company gave me that, I'd step aside gracefully. Without it I'd cling to the job, I'm not ashamed to say.

say: I'd say this is a **catastrophe** and governments and firms did nothing with years of warning.
I'd say it **publicly** and in the union, which I rarely do.
think: I expect my whole job to be done by AI by **2028**, and the warehouse robots to follow.
I have **no plan**, and four months' savings won't bridge twelve years to my full pension.
do: Cut every expense, the **holiday** and the car swap.
Ask for an **early-retirement** and severance talk while they still need me.
Tell my team of four **plainly** what I think.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake doing sums on what four months' savings does against twelve years until the full pension.
fieldNote: He is **honest and protective** of his team, and wants to warn them rather than hide it.
His fear is **concrete and financial**: the gap between savings and the full pension.

steps.text: Cut the holiday and swap the car for a cheaper one
Ask the company for early-retirement and severance terms
Push the union for a binding agreement
Tell my team of four plainly what's coming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years and we must use them, start the talks on retraining and income support now. Online I'd say no firm should be allowed to cut a worker without notice. I'd say it calmly, as a campaign, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, but I'm still 63 when it lands, close enough to the end that I'd probably be pushed out early. The extra time helps if I use it, and I'm not good at changing quickly. That's my honest weakness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to pay down what's left on the house, rebuild the savings to six months, and sign my retirement paperwork to fall at 62 or 63. I'd still refuse the tools, but I'd write down everything I know about our suppliers and hand it to the team, since that's the part I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steadier kind. Five years is like seeing a storm on the forecast. You can board the windows, you can't stop it. Better than two years, still not good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What does the extra time actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time lets me finish paying the mortgage, which is the biggest thing. At 63 with no mortgage and six months saved, I'd be bruised but standing. That's the difference between a bad outcome and a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned retiring early. Would you move that date forward or hold it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold the date at 62 and make it a real plan. If the company wants me gone earlier, I'd want a deal, and I'd have the union press for it. I'm not going to hang on and let them make the choice for me.

say: I'd say **start retraining talks** and income support now, while we have years.
I'd argue no firm should cut workers **without notice**.
think: Five years helps, but I'd still be **63 when it lands**, and I change slowly.
I worry I'd be **pushed out early** before the pension is safe.
do: Pay off the **mortgage** and rebuild savings to six months.
Plan to retire at **62 or 63**, not later.
Write down my **supplier knowledge** and hand it to the team.
feel: **Anxious but steadier**, like seeing a storm on the forecast.
S3.quote: Five years is like seeing a storm on the forecast. You can board the windows, you can't stop it. Better than two years, still not good.
fieldNote: He treats extra time as **a chance** to fix money, not to retrain, and he plans around his own pension date.
His candid **self-knowledge about being slow** to change shapes every plan.

steps.text: Pay off the remaining mortgage before 2031
Set my retirement date at 62 or 63
Write down my supplier knowledge for the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a problem for the young, and the decent thing is to build their way through it. Schools, apprenticeships, public support. I'd say we should use the decade to write the rules, not wait for a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired by then, so I'm not afraid for myself. I'd be afraid for my children and the young buyers coming through. My own pension would be safe, which is why I'm a bit uncomfortable with how little I'm worrying about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, finish my career my way, and retire at 62 as planned. I'd spend my last years teaching the young buyers how to judge a supplier, which is the part a machine can't copy. Priya first. And I'd volunteer in the union's work on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm for me, a little uneasy for them. A long runway makes a world of difference, and I've done well in my career, so I can leave without fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years changes things for someone your age. What's different for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter is a teacher, my son works in logistics. I'd tell them not to wait to be told, to get close to the work AI can't do and to join a union. I'd sit with my son and go through what a decade really means for a warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to protect in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young team, definitely. Priya, her mates, my son. I'd share what I know, I'd stand up for them in the union, and I'd use my vote for anyone who promises a real plan. That's my small contribution.

say: I'd say the decade should be used to **write rules** and support the young.
I'd call for schools, apprenticeships and **public support** now.
think: I'd be **retired by then**, so my own pension is safe.
I'm uneasy about **how little I worry** for myself and how much for the young.
do: Spend my last years **mentoring Priya** on judging suppliers.
feel: **Fairly calm** for myself, uneasy for the young.
S4.quote: I'd spend my last years teaching the young buyers how to judge a supplier, which is the part a machine can't copy.
fieldNote: The long runway moves his worry **from himself** to the young.
He values **mentoring** and union work as his legacy, and this shows a generous, outward-looking side.

steps.text: Mentor the younger buyers on judging suppliers until I retire
Volunteer with the union's retraining programme
Vote for candidates with a real retraining plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the 2028 picture, worries me most. I'm 58, I've got a few months of savings, and a pension that isn't enough yet if I'm out early. What would help is real notice, a proper severance written down, and a union or something like it that sits across the table from the company. Retraining sounds nice, but at my age I need an income bridge to retirement, not a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stubborn for fun. I distrust a tool I can't see inside, because when it's wrong, nobody answers for it. I'd rather be paid fairly to hand over thirty years of judgement than have it quietly copied and me shown the door.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be paid fairly to hand over thirty years of judgement than have it quietly copied and me shown the door.
portrait: **Jamal** is 58, a senior hardware buyer at a building-supply distributor, with a partner and grown-up children.
He is **proud of his craft**, trusts phone calls and pencil over software, and has never used AI tools.
Progressive and **pro-union**, he blames owners and shareholders, not the technology itself, for what could go wrong.
His **cushion is thin**, so any early exit would hit hard before his pension is secure.
He grows more worried as the clock shortens, and wants **notice, severance** and a say more than retraining.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: he'd lose his job before his pension is secure and with little savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **long notice** and written severance, plus a union or similar body with real bargaining power.
